notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Nehemiah 7:25–49, based on the available sources.

---

## General Background to the List (vv. 6–73)

Before treating individual verses, nearly all commentators note several overarching points about this entire section (vv. 6–73):

- This is not a list of those who came with Nehemiah in 444 B.C. but a register of those who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua in **537 B.C.** under Cyrus. It is almost identical to the list in Ezra 2. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/7-25.html — Constable; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-25.htm — Keil & Delitzsch)
- Nehemiah discovered this old register while seeking to repopulate Jerusalem (7:5). The list served to establish who was a genuine Israelite, validate property claims, and encourage people to move into the city (Neh 11:1–2). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/7-25.html — Constable)
- Differences between this list and Ezra 2 are explained by Gill: the Ezra list was made in Babylon when people first enrolled; this list was compiled after arrival in Jerusalem. Some who enrolled changed their minds and stayed, some died en route, and others joined later — hence numbers vary. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-25.htm — Gill)
- Matthew Henry says the repetition of names and numbers in Scripture displays God’s delight in the persons, families, and services of His spiritual Israel. “He knows those that are his, knows them all, knows them by name.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/7-25.html — Henry)
- The list is divided into categories: (1) lay Israelites (vv. 7b–38), (2) priests (vv. 39–42), (3) Levites, singers, gatekeepers (vv. 43–45), (4) temple servants / Nethinim (vv. 46–56). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-7-commentary)

---

## The Lay Returnees Listed by Locality (vv. 25–38)

The Cambridge Bible notes a shift at v. 25: where earlier verses listed people by ancestral families (“the sons of…”), many of the following entries are listed **by place of origin** (“the men of…”), reflecting that these were people grouped by their ancestral towns. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/nehemiah/7.htm)

### v. 25 — “the descendants of Gibeon, 95”

- **Pulpit Commentary**: In Ezra 2:20 the name is “Gibbar,” a name otherwise unknown. “Gibeon” should probably be read in both places. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/7-25.html — Pulpit)
- **Cambridge Bible**: Agrees that “Gibeon” = “Gibbar” in Ezra, and that “Gibbar” is probably a mistake. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-25.htm — Cambridge)
- **Geneva Study Bible**: Reads this as “the inhabitants of Gibeon.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-25.htm)
- **Pett**: Notes that “Gibbar” means “hero.” The Nehemiah list may be transferring them to a list enrolled by domicile — linking the family to the city of Gibeon. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)
- **Clarke**: Does not add further here but refers readers to his notes on Ezra 2 for the parallel. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/nehemiah/7.htm)

### v. 26 — “the men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188”

- **Cambridge Bible**: In Ezra 2:21–22 these are listed as “the children of Beth-lehem…the men of Netophah” (123 + 56 = 179). Here they are combined into one figure, 188. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-26.htm)
- **Gill**: Netophah was a town near Bethlehem in Judah. The combined figure of 188 differs from the separate Ezra totals — reflecting the different circumstances under which each register was compiled. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-26.htm)
- Bethlehem is, of course, the city of David and the future birthplace of the Messiah. Commentators do not press this in Nehemiah 7, but the Davidic connection underlies the significance of the town.

### v. 27 — “the men of Anathoth, 128”

- Anathoth was a priestly city in Benjamin, the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 1:1). No commentator in the consulted sources expands on this specifically for v. 27, but the town’s identity as a Levitical city (Josh 21:18) is well known.

### v. 28 — “the men of Beth-azmaveth, 42”

- A small Benjamite town near Jerusalem (cf. Ezra 2:24, where it is “Azmaveth”). The number 42 is identical in both lists.

### v. 29 — “the men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743”

- These three towns are grouped together as one returning community — all situated in the territory of Benjamin / the Gibeonite confederation. Kiriath-jearim was where the Ark of the Covenant rested before David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Sam 7:1–2). The Ezra 2:25 figure matches at 743.

### v. 30 — “the men of Ramah and Geba, 621”

- Ramah and Geba were Benjamite towns. Ramah features prominently in the narratives of Samuel and in the return from exile (Jer 40:1). The town names are identical in Ezra 2:26, though Ezra gives 623 to the separate entry for Ramah and Geba combined.

### v. 31 — “the men of Michmash, 122”

- Michmash (Michmas) was the site of Jonathan’s famous victory over the Philistines (1 Sam 13–14). The number 122 matches Ezra 2:27.

### v. 32 — “the men of Bethel and Ai, 123”

- Bethel (“house of God”) and Ai (“ruin”) are famous from the patriarchal narratives (Gen 12:8; 28:19) and the conquest under Joshua (Josh 7–8). The number 123 matches Ezra 2:28.

### v. 33 — “the men of the other Nebo, 52”

- **Clarke**: The word “other” (Hebrew *acher*) is not in the parallel passage in Ezra 2:29, and is missing from many Hebrew manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi. This Nebo is thought to be the same as Nob or Nobah, in the tribe of Benjamin. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/nehemiah/7.htm)
- **Cambridge Bible**: Suggests “other” may have come in accidentally from v. 34. Ezra simply has “the children of Nebo.” (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/nehemiah/7.htm)
- **Pett**: Notes the town may have been called “Nebo Acher” to distinguish it from Nebo in Reuben (Num 32:3, 38). It may be represented by Beit Nuba, about 12 miles northwest of Jerusalem. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)

### v. 34 — “the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254”

- **Clarke**: “The other Elam” — to distinguish this family from the Elam already mentioned in v. 12 (which had 1,254 — the same number, coincidentally). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/nehemiah/7.htm)
- **Pett**: “Elam Acher” may actually be the name of a Benjamite town (a Benjamite named Elam is mentioned in 1 Chr 8:24). The writer has reverted to “the sons of…” phrasing, but from its context among Benjamite towns, it likely denotes domicile. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)

### v. 35 — “the descendants of Harim, 320”

- The number 320 matches Ezra 2:32. (A different Harim appears among the priests in v. 42 below.)

### v. 36 — “the men of Jericho, 345”

- Jericho, the first city conquered in Canaan (Josh 6), had been resettled. The number 345 matches Ezra 2:34.

### v. 37 — “the men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 721”

- These towns lay in the coastal plain / Shephelah region, northwest of Jerusalem. Lod (Lydda) appears in the New Testament (Acts 9:32). The number is 721 in Nehemiah; Ezra 2:33 has 725.

### v. 38 — “the descendants of Senaah, 3,930”

- Senaah is the largest group in the entire lay list. The number 3,930 matches Ezra 2:35 at 3,630 — one of the larger discrepancies between the two lists. Gill attributes such variations to the different times of registration. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-25.htm — Gill)

---

## The Priests (vv. 39–42)

### v. 39 — “The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah (through the house of Jeshua), 973”

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: Notes that only **four of the twenty-four priestly courses** established by David returned from the captivity. (The course of Abijah, mentioned in Luke 1:5, is not in this list.) These four courses were later subdivided again into twenty-four, which retained the original Davidic names. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/nehemiah/7.htm)
- **Enduring Word**: The priests were essential to worship. Their listing (with specific numbers for each house) shows that God values those who lead worship and that their service is recorded before Him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-7/)
- Jedaiah’s connection “through the house of Jeshua” links this priestly family to the high-priestly line of Jeshua (Joshua) the son of Jozadak, who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2; Hag 1:1).

### v. 40 — “the descendants of Immer, 1,052”

- Immer was one of the original twenty-four priestly courses (1 Chr 24:14). The number 1,052 matches Ezra 2:37.

### v. 41 — “the descendants of Pashhur, 1,247”

- Pashhur was another of the twenty-four courses. The name is associated with a priest who opposed Jeremiah (Jer 20:1–6). The number 1,247 matches Ezra 2:38.

### v. 42 — “the descendants of Harim, 1,017”

- Harim was the third of the four priestly courses listed. (A separate, lay Harim appears in v. 35 above.) The number 1,017 matches Ezra 2:39.

- **General observation on the priests**: Matthew Henry notes that the priests’ genealogy was especially important because no one could serve at the altar without proven descent from Aaron. This is why Nehemiah later excluded those whose genealogical records were lost (vv. 63–65). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/7-25.html — Henry)

---

## The Levites, Singers, and Gatekeepers (vv. 43–45)

### v. 43 — “The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua (through Kadmiel, through the line of Hodevah), 74.”

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The phrasing “the children of Jeshua, of Kadmiel, and of the children of Hodevah” may be corrected from Ezra 2:40 and Ezra 3:9 to read “Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodevah.” The ancestor Hodevah appears under three forms: Hodevah (here), Hodaviah (Ezra 2:40), and Judah (Ezra 3:9). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-43.htm)
- **Pett**: Strikingly, only **74 Levites** returned compared to 4,289 priests. This imbalance is explained by the fact that Levites had been less prominent in pre-exilic society — many had not been exiled, and those who were had less incentive to return, since they only assisted priests. Ezra 8:15 confirms their reluctance: “I viewed the people and the priests, and found there none of the sons of Levi.” Jeshua and Kadmiel had been chiefs of two orders of Levites who oversaw the workmen on the Temple in Zerubbabel’s day (Ezra 3:9). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)

### v. 44 — “The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 148.”

- **Pett**: The singers were a special order of Levites responsible for leading singing and musical accompaniment in Temple worship. Asaph is mentioned in 1 Chr 6:39. Of the three musical orders from Solomon’s time (Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun/Ethan — 2 Chr 5:12), only the sons of Asaph returned at this stage. In Ezra 3:10–11, the sons of Asaph led worship with cymbals at the foundation-laying of the new Temple. The number here is 148; Ezra 2:41 gives 128. The increase may be due to comings of age or additional singers returning later. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)
- **BibleHub Study**: The Asaphite singers are “essential support staff for worship.” (https://www.biblehub.com/study/chapters/nehemiah/7.htm)

### v. 45 — “The gatekeepers: … 138 in all.”

- Six families of gatekeepers are listed: Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai.
- **Pett**: The gatekeepers were another special order of Levites responsible for opening the Temple doors each morning, watching over the chambers and treasuries, guarding the vessels of service, and managing the fine flour, wine, oil, frankincense, and spices (1 Chr 9:17–30). Three of the six families (Shallum, Talmon, Akkub) are descended from gatekeepers mentioned in 1 Chr 9:17 who dwelt in pre-exilic Jerusalem. The number 138 here represents a reduction of one from Ezra 2:42 (139), likely due to deaths or comings of age between the two registers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)
- **Pett also notes** (in his comments on Neh 7:1–3) that Nehemiah later appointed these same gatekeepers to guard the city gates as well — because they were the men already trained and experienced in guard duties. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)

---

## The Temple Servants / Nethinim (vv. 46–49)

### v. 46 — “The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth”

- **Precept Austin**: Cross-references the Nethinim to Josh 9:23–27 (the Gibeonites made “hewers of wood and drawers of water” for the sanctuary), 1 Chr 9:2, and Lev 27:2–8. The Nethinim were “given ones” — temple assistants first assigned by David and the leaders (Ezra 8:20). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-7-commentary)
- **Pett**: The Nethinim probably had their initial origin in the Gibeonites of Joshua 9:27. They were later supplemented by prisoners of war and other slaves whom David and the princes “gave for the service of the Levites” (Ezra 8:20). Their name means “given ones” — given to God for temple service. Despite their humble origins, they had their own quarters in Jerusalem (Neh 3:26, 31), were exempt from taxes (Ezra 7:24), and took the oath of the covenant alongside all Israel (Neh 10:28–31). That so many Nethinim chose to return from exile (compared to the small number of Levites) shows they valued their role in God’s house. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-7.html)
- **BibleHub Study**: The listing of the Nethinim “shows the continuity of humble service.” (https://www.biblehub.com/study/chapters/nehemiah/7.htm)

### v. 47 — “the descendants of Keros, the descendants of Sia, the descendants of Padon”

- **JFB / Pulpit**: “Sia” in Nehemiah 7:47 is the same as “Siaha” in Ezra 2:44 — another example of name variation between the two registers, attributable to Jewish custom of individuals bearing more than one name. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/nehemiah/7.htm)
- **Pulpit**: The Neh 7 Nethinim list is very close to Ezra 2:43–54; a few names are differently spelt, and one name from Ezra (Akkub, Ezra 2:45) is omitted here. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-46.htm)

### v. 48 — “the descendants of Lebanah, the descendants of Hagabah, the descendants of Shalmai”

- No specific commentary from the consulted sources singles out these names individually, beyond noting they belong to the Nethinim families who returned.

### v. 49 — “the descendants of Hanan, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Gahar”

- As with v. 48, these are part of the Nethinim catalogue. Giddel (גִּדֵּל) appears again among “Solomon’s servants” in v. 58 (a different Giddel). Gahar is consistently named in both Ezra 2:47 and here.

---

## Points of Broader Theological Emphasis

Because vv. 25–49 are a genealogical list, traditional Protestant traditions do not diverge sharply on the meaning of individual verses. However, their respective teachers emphasise different **theological frameworks** for reading the list as a whole:

- **Reformed (JFB, Matthew Henry)**: Emphasise God’s sovereign providence — Nehemiah “ascribes not to his own prudence…but to the grace of God prompting and directing him.” The preserved genealogy shows God faithfully keeping His covenant people through exile so that the Messianic line would continue. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/nehemiah/7.htm)
- **Baptist (Gill)**: Gill stresses the historical precision — explaining numerical and name differences between Ezra and Nehemiah as arising from two registrations taken at different moments. No allegorical or spiritualising reading; the focus is on the factual integrity of the text. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/7-25.htm)
- **Methodist/Wesleyan (Clarke)**: Clarke attends carefully to manuscript evidence — noting, for example, that “other” in “the other Nebo” (v. 33) is missing in many Hebrew MSS collated by Kennicott and De Rossi. He also identifies the likely geographical locations of obscure towns. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/nehemiah/7.htm)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)**: The list is read devotionally — each name represents an individual with “a pioneer spirit” who “was willing to endure hardship and discomfort because they had a call from God.” The practical application is that God keeps a “book of remembrance” (Mal 3:16), and “nothing about God’s people is too small or insignificant to be recorded.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-7/)
- **Dispensational/Evangelical (Constable)**: Constable views the list historically — it is the record of the first return under Zerubbabel in 537 B.C., not of Nehemiah’s own generation. It serves as a second witness to God’s faithfulness and was the basis for Nehemiah’s later repopulation plan (Neh 11). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/7-25.html — Constable)

**Catholic and Orthodox sources**: No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on these individual verses was found among the allowed sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). The passage is a genealogical register and does not feature prominently in doctrinal or liturgical reading from those traditions.

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey)**: No results specific to these verses were retrieved from the limited searches available.
